turn_text: Thank you. Thank you for having me.

Let me ask you about your view of the House Agriculture Committee. You are from an urban district in Ohio and you sit on that committee. Do you feel like that it is a place that you can have a positive input and impact on this farm bill?

Absolutely. You know, people do think it's a little odd that I'm from Cleveland and I sit on the committee. But let me just suggest to you that I am excited about the opportunity to give a different view from what they, under normal circumstances, would get that the committee has historically been very farm-based. And I think that when you look at agriculture, it encompasses so many more things. So I'm just happy to be a part of broadening the perspective and the discussion about what kinds of things we can do with the farm bill.

The Farm Bill as the House Agriculture Committee passed it apparently wasn't what you wanted as it shows that you voted against that. Could you tell me what it was about the bill that made you vote no? I

voted against it and I spoke against it as well. One of the major issues for me clearly was a $16 billion cut to SNAP as well as the change in the eligibility requirements to qualify for SNAP. And there were some other things as well, certainly as it relates to 1890 institutions and other things, but in particular, my biggest concern was that you cannot, in this economy, cut $16 billion from SNAP. So that was my biggest issue with the bill.

You had some allies in that there were some Republicans who felt like there weren't nearly enough cuts to SNAP to the point that Congressman Holskamp was kicked off the committee for this coming term i wonder what that shows of extremes on both sides and uh... both of you uh... not wanting to let a bill like this go through

well uh... let me just first say that i don't believe that the congressman was was removed from the committee because he voted against the farm bill i think that was a wholly different situation with a different message uh... but more importantly you're right but there is has been a lot of discussion that uh... that the SNAP pieces or the nutrition pieces need to be separated from the farm bill and look that differently. But because it is not that way right now, the only way that we can address the situation is to vote against it. Yes, there are people that think that it wasn't enough cuts, but let me just suggest to you this. The Senate only cut $4.5 billion out of there in their bill for SNAP. We turn around and do $16 billion. When you look at the fact that almost 8% of the US population is unemployed, and that the current poverty rate is the second highest has been in 45 years. You can't talk about not feeding hungry children and hungry families. And when you look at the effects of SNAP, about 75% of all SNAP recipients are families with young children. And the other 25% are seniors or people with disabilities. So what is it that we are to do? Are we to say that as a nation, We are going to refuse to feed hungry people. We just say as a nation that we are not concerned about the nutrition of our children. I don't think that people understand the consequences of making those kinds of decisions unless they live in environments like mine.

turn_text: The number of people who are qualified for portions of the food and nutrition program now has gone up very sharply in the last four years. Do you credit that to a worsening economy or to more liberal policies under the Obama administration?

Well, absolutely. It is the direct result of a worsening economy. I mean, clearly, I mean, no one. Do you think that that I would want for people to be on food stamps. I would hope that people wouldn't be, because that would say to me that the economy was growing, that people are working, people are more comfortable. We want to get to a point where the allocations for food stamps are reduced significantly, but this is not the time at which to do it.

You have been critical of the obesity of young people and have dedicated yourself to try to overcome that in one generation. It seems almost a contradiction that we have obesity because of people being short of money and the strangeness of that in our society that hunger and obesity are not simple problems to fix.

You are correct and I have to as well have this same discussion with my colleagues because they would make the same argument to me. But if they look at the many of the issues that surround obesity and I will just just count some of them off for you. Most poor people live in environments where they can't even access healthy food. If you have a grocery store that is two miles from you and you have no access to either public transportation or an automobile, what you do is you go to these What we call corner stores or you go to places where the food is not healthy or more importantly what you do is you go to fast food restaurants where the nutrition value is meal and the calorie count and the fat count are way up. That's one of the issues which is what we call food death if you live in some of these environments and it happens not just in cities it happens in rural communities as well. When you look at the fact that most poor children and many rural children as well, urban and rural, get 90% of their nutrition from schools. So if their school meals are not nutritious, then they are not going to be healthy. You also look at the fact that we cut back on education funding. One of the very first things they cut back on is physical education. So you don't have young people who are being physically fit because they are not getting exercise. In environments like mine, there are children who don't even walk to school for fear of their own lives. So how do you say that the two are not connected? I further want to say that obesity is an epidemic in this country. We have almost 17% of the young population of this country today who are not physically or will not ever be physically fit to serve in the military. Not because of necessarily just poverty, but it is what they eat. It is what we focus on in school. And is there lack of physical exercise?

turn_text: Representative Fudge, let me finish up with going back to the Farm Bill and asking you how that you think we should position this to where that a legislation can go into effect to keep us from having all the problems that would exist if we had to go back to the permanent legislation and yet make it palatable to you and to others to get a majority vote.

And I don't want to pit urban and rural against each other, but if you look at something as simple as the crop safety net, okay? Today, most of those farmers are gone. What we have is metacorporations who are making more money than they have ever made. I understand that there's some things we need to do in conservation. We can save some resources there.
